pairs.question: Quos, callide, motus quamue fugam moliris? nil transit amantes. sentio, peruigiles acuunt suspiria questus, numquam in pace sopor. quotiens haec ora natare fletibus et magnas latrantia pectora curas admota deprendo manu! nil foedere rupto conubiisue super moueor uiduaque iuuenta, etsi crudus amor necdum post flammea toti intepuere tori: tua me, properabo fateri, angit, amate, salus. tune incomitatus, inermis regna petes? poterisque tuis decedere Thebis, si neget? atque illum sollers deprendere semper Fama duces tumidum narrat raptoque superbum difficilemque tibi: necdum consumpserat annum. me quoque nunc uates, nunc exta minantia diuos aut auium lapsus aut turbida noctis imago terret et (a, memini!) numquam mihi falsa per umbras Iuno uenit. quo tendis iter? ni conscius ardor ducit et ad Thebas melior socer.
pairs.answer: Solue metus animo, dabitur, mihi crede, merentum consiliis tranquilla dies; te fortior annis nondum cura decet.
pairs.derivation: Argia, sensing Polynices plotting a departure, addresses him in bed; her whole speech is one extended interrogative plea (quos motus...moliris? tune...regna petes? quo tendis iter?), quoted contiguous and verbatim with the interspersed speech tag 'ait' (after 'moliris?') dropped as framing, and the opening 'quos' capitalized. Polynices' reply is introduced by narration (hic breue tandem risit... lacrimasque repressit:), which is cut. The answer is the operative opening of his reply, to the first full stop after 'nondum cura decet'; what follows ('sciat haec Saturnius olim...' and the promise 'fors aderit lux illa tibi...') elaborates and is cut. The semicolon after 'dies' is interior and kept.
